sections.title: Definition & Clinical Overview
sections.content: Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome (AWS) is a hyper-excitable state of the central nervous system that occurs when a chronic, heavy drinker suddenly ceases or significantly reduces ethanol intake. It ranges from mild tremulousness to life-threatening Delirium Tremens (DTs). In the ophthalmic context, AWS is critical due to its association with Wernicke Encephalopathy, characterized by ophthalmoplegia, nystagmus, and ataxia.

branches: Chronic Alcohol: Potentiates GABA (Inhibitory), Inhibits NMDA (Excitatory)
Adaptation: Down-regulation of GABA receptors, Up-regulation of NMDA receptors
Withdrawal: Massive loss of GABAergic inhibition + NMDA-mediated glutamate surge

sections.title: Chronological Progression of Symptoms
content: 6-12 Hours: Mild symptoms (Insomnia, tremulousness, mild anxiety, GI upset, headache, diaphoresis, palpitations).
12-24 Hours: Alcoholic Hallucinosis (Visual, auditory, or tactile hallucinations; sensorium is clear).
24-48 Hours: Withdrawal Seizures (Generalized tonic-clonic; usually singular or in short bursts).
48-96 Hours: Delirium Tremens (Clouded consciousness, extreme autonomic hyperactivity, severe tremors, fever).

sections.title: The Ocular Examination: Wernicke’s Focus
content: Horizontal Gaze-Evoked Nystagmus (Most common ocular sign)
Abducens (CN VI) Nerve Palsy: Often bilateral, but can be asymmetrical
Conjugate Gaze Palsy: Inability to move eyes in tandem vertically or horizontally
Sluggish Pupillary Light Response or Miosis
Papilledema (Rare, but indicates severe encephalopathy)
Retinal Hemorrhages (Usually secondary to associated thrombocytopenia or trauma)

content.explanation: C: Confusion (Encephalopathy); A: Ataxia (Gait instability); N: Nystagmus (and Ophthalmoplegia). If untreated, it progresses to Korsakoff Psychosis (Anterograde/Retrograde amnesia + Confabulation).

rows: 0 (None) to 7 (Severe, even with arms not extended)
Goiter, exophthalmos, elevated T4/T3, suppressed TSH

sections.title: EMERGENCY: Delirium Tremens (DTs)
content: Severe autonomic instability (Tachycardia >120, BP >160/100)
Profound hyperthermia (Fever >38.5°C / 101.3°F)
Fluctuating level of consciousness and severe disorientation
Vivid, often terrifying 'zoopsia' (hallucinations of small animals/insects)
DANGER: High risk of cardiovascular collapse or status epilepticus

sections.title: Investigations & Diagnostic Workup
content: 1. Laboratory: CBC (Macrocytosis, Thrombocytopenia), BMP (Electrolytes, Anion gap), LFTs (AST:ALT > 2:1), Blood Alcohol Level (BAL).
2. Nutritional Screen: Serum B1 (Thiamine) level (often low), Mg2+ (critical to correct for B1 response).
3. Imaging: CT Head if first-time seizure or trauma; MRI Brain (T2/FLAIR hyperintensities in mammillary bodies for Wernicke's).
4. ECG: Evaluate for QTc prolongation (risk of Torsades de Pointes).

sections.title: Management Strategy: Step-by-Step
content: 1. Stabilization: Airway protection and IV access.
2. Thiamine Replacement: 500mg IV TID for 2 days, then 250mg daily. GIVE BEFORE GLUCOSE.
3. Symptom-Triggered BZDs: Diazepam or Lorazepam based on CIWA-Ar scores.
4. Fluid/Electrolyte Correction: Replace Magnesium (target >2.0 mg/dL) and Potassium.
5. Supportive Care: Quiet, dimly lit room; frequent reorientation.

rows: Preferred in liver failure or elderly (short half-life).
Commonly used for outpatient/mild withdrawal tapers.

Adjunct for autonomic control; does not treat underlying GABA deficit.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Thiamine deficiency causes mitochondrial dysfunction; glucose infusion without Thiamine exacerbates pyruvate accumulation, worsening Wernicke's.
Abducens palsy in AWS is often the most responsive sign to Thiamine, resolving within hours to days.
Ataxia may take weeks to improve, and 50% of patients have permanent gait deficits.
Kindling Effect: Each subsequent withdrawal episode is more severe and carries a higher risk of seizures/DTs.

sections.title: Landmark Evidence: The ASAM Guidelines
sections.content: The American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Clinical Practice Guideline recommends 'Symptom-Triggered' therapy over 'Fixed-Schedule' therapy for BZDs in AWS. This approach reduces the total dose of medication used and the duration of treatment, provided the patient can be monitored frequently using the CIWA-Ar scale.

sections.title: Red Flag: Refractory AWS
content: Requirement of >50mg Diazepam or >10mg Lorazepam in first hour
Failure to respond to high-dose BZDs suggests need for Phenobarbital or Propofol
Escalate to ICU level care immediately
